Annoying Habits That Are Actually Cries for Help

  • Most dog owners have dealt with at least one of these behaviors, and itâs tempting to see them simply as bad habits.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

According to recent reports, dogs are easy to love but, on occasion, are also surprisingly difficult to live with. Barking for no reason. The leash pulling that turns a simple walk into a tug-of-war. Turning the most expensive thing in the room into a chew toyâ¦.

Most dog owners have dealt with at least one of these behaviors, and itâs tempting to see them simply as bad habits. But the truth is, there is often a reason behind these irritating habits. Dogs communicate through behavior, and what looks like a nuisance is sometimes a symptom of an unmet need. The trouble is that we often get distracted by tackling that symptom when we really need to dig deeper.

Understanding what is driving an annoying or unwanted behavior can make it much easier to address.

Recent findings suggest that dogs bark for many reasons, including boredom, anxiety, fear, a perceived threat, or a desire for attention. Any dog can develop a barking habit, regardless of size.

Recent findings suggest that the key is identifying what triggers it. Boredom-related barking may improve with more exercise and mental stimulation, while anxiety or fear-based barking generally requires a more structured approach. Teaching a reliable "quiet" command and avoiding accidentally rewarding attention-seeking barking can also help.

Recent findings suggest that naturally vigilant dogs that spend their days standing guard at windows and alerting you to every passerby or suspicious-looking trash can may become less anxious if you block or obscure their view of the street. Limiting access to front-facing rooms or applying privacy film to windows can be a simple solution â if they canât see it, they stop worrying about it.

Chewing is normal for dogs, particularly teething puppies, but it becomes a problem when furniture, clothing, carpets, or walls become the preferred targets.

Boredom and anxiety can contribute to destructive chewing, as can a lack of appropriate outlets. Keeping suitable chew toys available, putting valuable items out of reach, and managing the environment while the dog learns what is acceptable can help redirect the habit.

Recent findings suggest that A dog that greets visitors by launching itself at them has usually learned that jumping gets a response. Even pushing the dog away or telling it to stop can give them the attention theyâre seeking.

Sources indicate that ignoring the jumping and rewarding calm, four-paws-on-the-floor behavior teaches the dog that staying down gets the better response. Giving the dog an alternative behavior, such as sitting, can make the lesson clearer.

When faced with a friendly jumping dog, try the following:.

Keep your arms crossed, mouth closed, and eyes averted.

Turn your back, and walk away if they keep jumping.

Ignore them until they are calm and ready to listen to your command.

It has been revealed that dogs beg because it has worked before. Even one successful attempt at getting food from the table can establish the habit, making it particularly difficult to break.

Sources indicate that feeding the dog before your mealtimes can reduce the motivation to beg, while teaching it to settle in a designated spot gives it something else to do. The biggest challenge is consistency. Giving in occasionally can keep the behavior going.

Table scraps can also pose health risks because some common human foods are harmful to dogs, while regular extras can contribute to obesity.

It has been revealed that leash pulling can make an otherwise enjoyable walk exhausting. Dogs often pull because they are excited and have not learned that pulling does not make the walk happen faster.

Recent findings suggest that loose-leash training takes patience. Stopping whenever the leash becomes tight and continuing only when it becomes slack teaches the dog what behavior allows the walk to continue. Rewarding the dog for walking beside the handler can reinforce the lesson, while a well-fitted harness may provide additional control during training.

According to recent reports, different dogs need different equipment, and what works for a small dog is not necessarily going to be suitable for a large one. Talk to your vet about the safest and most effective option for you and your dog.

Poor recall is frustrating, but it can also be dangerous if your dog runs towards traffic or another dog.

Sources indicate that training should start in areas with few distractions before gradually becoming more challenging. High-value rewards can make coming back more appealing, while using the recall command for unpleasant situations can create a negative association that undermines the training.

Digging is instinctive for many dogs and can also be linked to boredom or excess energy. Trying to eliminate the behavior completely may not be the most practical approach; redirection has a much higher chance of success.

Create a designated digging area, such as a sandbox or corner of the yard, making sure there is a clear distinction between this and the rest of the garden. It may be unsightly, but laying down some temporary netting or a similar obstacle in the rest of the yard can help teach your dog where they can and cannot dig. Burying toys or treats there can make the spot more appealing, while increasing daily activity may reduce the urge to dig elsewhere.

In a recent development, some dogs struggle when left alone. The resulting distress can include destructive behavior, excessive barking, and other difficult behaviors.

Gradually getting a dog used to being alone, starting with very short absences and slowly increasing them, is an evidence-based approach. Providing a comfortable, safe space can also help.

Avoid making a fuss of your dog when leaving the house or on your return â your comings and goings should become part of an ordinary day, not an event. More severe cases of separation anxiety may require veterinary input or help from a behaviorist.

Industry observers note that aggression can have many possible causes, including fear, poor socialization, pain, territorial behavior, or negative past experiences. Because the appropriate response depends on the cause, this is one behavior where professional help is particularly important.

According to recent reports, A veterinary examination can help rule out an underlying medical problem, including pain. A qualified trainer or behaviorist can then help address the behavior using approaches such as positive reinforcement, desensitization, and counterconditioning. Punishment can make aggression worse rather than better.

Occasional accidents can happen, but frequent or sudden indoor elimination deserves attention.

Recent findings suggest that for dogs that are still learning, regular bathroom breaks and immediate positive reinforcement for going outside provide the foundation for housetraining. Enzymatic cleaners are useful for removing waste odors that can otherwise encourage a dog to return to the same spot.

If a previously house-trained dog suddenly begins having accidents, a check-up at the vet is appropriate to check for a possible medical cause.

Barking, chewing, jumping, digging, and the other behaviors on this list may be frustrating, but they rarely happen without a reason. Looking at what a dog is trying to communicate can reveal whether it needs more activity, clearer training, or a different kind of attention.

Addressing the underlying matter rather than simply trying to stop the behavior can make the problem easier to manage and help strengthen the relationship between you and your dog.

In this episode of Catsterâs Chatty Cattys podcast, hosts Nicole and Dr. Karyn jump into an unstructured, wide-ranging discussion covering quirky pet habits, feline anatomy, and the ethics of animal testing vs. clinical research. From explaining the post-poop "zoomies" to reflecting on how decades-old feline nerve studies shed light on why cats freeze in harnesses, the hosts offer a lighthearted yet insightful look into how our pets interact with the world.

Discover the fascinating science behind feline movement, including how lower-body nerve pathways allow cats to adjust their bodies instinctively without waiting for brain signals. Dr. Karyn also breaks down why putting a coat or harness on a cat disrupts this "sixth sense," causing them to initially freeze or flop over.

Additionally, the hosts explore the difference between historical animal testing and modern, mutually beneficial clinical trials. From discussing how research into feline coronavirus treatments surprisingly overlapped with human health developments to debating why testing food or drugs on animals can be unreliable (imagine if chocolate was banned because it was tested on dogs!), this episode balances fun pet owner anecdotes with fascinating veterinary science.

It has been revealed that the Mystery of "Poop Zoomies": Nicole and Dr. Karyn talk about how cats often sprint out of the litter box after taking a poop. They discuss how this hilarious habit stems from a mix of wild instinct (running from scent markers) and sheer physical relief.

In a recent development, do Cats Always Land on Their Feet?: While cats try to land on their feet using their incredible spinal flexibility, Dr. Karyn notes it isn't an absolute ruleâpointing out that her own cat, Clutch, occasionally falls right on his butt.

It has been revealed that how Feline Nerves Act Like a "Body Brain": Dr. Karyn discusses an old study on feline nerve pathways showing that cats can walk on a treadmill via spinal reflexes without upper brain input. This ultra-fast neural feedback gives cats rapid spatial awareness.

Why Cats Freeze in Harnesses: Because a cat's body relies heavily on sensory feedback from skin and nerves for orientation, placing clothes or a harness on them is like "blindfolding" their body, causing them to temporarily lose balance until they adapt.

Testing vs. Clinical Trials: The hosts differentiate between harmful animal testing and ethical clinical research. Modern veterinary trials often involve treating pet patients with naturally occurring conditions (like cancer or coronavirus), generating medical advancements that aid both humans and animals.

Interspecies Differences in Testing: The hosts touch on why testing human items on animals can be flawed, pointing out that many things safe for humans (like chocolate, grapes, or garlic) are toxic to pets, and vice versa.

Stop Wasting Time and Money on These 7 Fall Lawn Care Jobs – Here's What Your Grass Really Needs

📅 19 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 6 min read (1177 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Gardeningknowhow

⏱️ ~6 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • Fall is a time of transition in the garden, not just for perennials, shrubs, and trees, but also for your grass.
  • Recent findings suggest that fall lawn care is all about working smarter, not harder.
  • Industry observers note that this year, focus your fall lawn care on a few smart tasks that help prepare the soil and roots for winter.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Fall is a time of transition in the garden, not just for perennials, shrubs, and trees, but also for your grass. Cool-season grasses perk up a little after the heat of midsummer, but now they’re getting ready for winter dormancy. Some of the tasks you might feel compelled to do now are unnecessary or even harmful.

Recent findings suggest that fall lawn care is all about working smarter, not harder. More fertilizer, more water, and more cutting can do more harm than good this time of year. There is a persistent myth that more care is better, but the truth is that many homeowners do too much.

Industry observers note that this year, focus your fall lawn care on a few smart tasks that help prepare the soil and roots for winter. Here is a list of typical chores you can skip this year and what to do instead. I promise, this will make your life a lot easier, and your lawn will thank you.

According to recent reports, many homeowners love the look of a pristinely green fall lawn. Others think keeping it totally clear of fall leaves is critical to the turf's health. Keeping the lawn totally clear can be backbreaking work, and it’s not worth the effort.

Sources indicate that it’s true that a dense layer of leaves, especially wet leaves, can harm the grass by trapping moisture and blocking sunlight. But some leaves left in place won’t smother the grass. Also, it’s unnecessary to physically remove every leaf.

Instead of endlessly raking, run a mulching mower, like this Greenworks model, over the grass as needed, chopping up the leaves when you see light to moderate coverage. Another option is to remove some of a thick layer of leaves for use in compost or as a mulch in beds. Don’t worry about removing every last leaf before winter.

Fall lawns typically need less supplemental water than summer lawns, so ditch your routine watering chore and play it by ear instead. Cooler fall temperatures reduce evaporation, so unless you have unusually dry conditions, you shouldn’t have to water lawns as often as in summer.

A simple rain gauge, such as this easy-to-read JMBay model from Amazon, can help you keep track of rainfall. Keep an eye on the soil and rain and decide when the grass could use a deep drink rather than sticking with a strict schedule.

In a recent development, of course, there are exceptions. If you have seeded parts of the lawn or installed new sod before winter, these areas should be watered regularly right up until the ground freezes.

Recent findings suggest that at some point, there will be a final mow of the season, but strategy to keep cutting regularly until the grass stops actively growing. Until then, don’t cut grass too short. Your turf needs substantial foliage to collect energy from the sun and build strong, deep roots. Cutting grass short leads to shorter roots, which struggle more through the winter than long roots.

Recent findings suggest that keep mowing to the recommended height for your type of grass until the final cut. A tool like the Oregon Deck Leveling Gauge from Amazon can help you check your mower's cutting height and ensure an even cut.

As growth slows, you’ll need to cut less frequently. When it’s time to make the final cut, use the lower end of the recommended height range for the grass. It should be at a medium height for winter.

Recent findings suggest that bagging all of your healthy grass clippings is unnecessary. It’s also a highly labor-intensive chore. Don’t waste your time, energy, or back on this one. Finely chopped grass decomposes promptly and adds nutrients to the soil. And, contrary to popular belief, grass clippings left on the ground do not contribute to thatch buildup.

Instead of bagging cut grass, use a mulching mower. You might want to pick up some of the grass if you have a lot of heavy clumps sitting on the lawn, but most can be kept in place to decompose. The more frequently you mow, the fewer big clumps you'll get.

Managing weeds in the turf can be a useful fall chore, giving your grass a better chance of getting nutrients and water as it prepares for winter dormancy. However, it’s possible to overwork this chore. Many annual weeds will die as temperatures drop, so don’t bother with these.

In a recent development, instead, focus your energy on managing tough perennial weeds. Examples include dandelions, plantain, and clover. Fall is a good time to tackle these with a selective post-emergent herbicide, such as Ortho WeedClear Lawn Weed Killer, provided the weeds are still actively growing and the product is suitable for your grass type. Alternatively, pull them by hand with a tool like Grampa's Weeder, which removes deep-rooted weeds without the need to bend down.

Fall fertilizing can benefit a lawn, but applying fertilizer automatically or getting the product or timing wrong can waste time and money, or even harm your grass. Warm-season grass is going dormant now, so feeding it can trigger growth that only gets damaged in cooler weather.

Recent findings suggest that cool-season grass is different. It’s gathering and storing nutrients in fall and also recovering from summer stress. Fertilizing now can be beneficial if the grass is still growing and the ground hasn't frozen, but be sure to use the right product. You can find fall-specific feeds at garden centers, often called winterizer fertilizers. One popular option is Scotts Turf Builder WinterGuard Fall Lawn Food, which helps lawns recover from summer stress and develop stronger roots ahead of winter.

According to recent reports, your lawn doesn’t have to look perfectly green and manicured in fall to be healthy. Trying to remove every stick, branch, and leaf from the turf is wasted energy. It’s a thankless chore that won’t improve turf health. In fact, leaving some natural material in place benefits the local ecosystem. Next year’s pollinators could be hiding in the leaf litter or the hollowed stem of a fallen branch.

Instead of aiming for perfection, target your efforts at thinning thick mats of leaves, clearing walkways and drainage areas, and creating designated natural areas. Leave some corners of the garden undisturbed, where wildlife can shelter and survive the winter. Aim for a healthy lawn, not a sterile landscape.

Sources indicate that as you initiative fall lawn chores, remember that type of grass matters. Know what kind of grass you have and what it needs in terms of fall fertilizer, weed protection, and mowing. All homeowners want to give their grass its best chance to come out healthy and green in the spring, but be smart about fall chores. Be selective about your efforts this time of year and focus on those tasks that will actually make a difference to the health of your lawn.

Mary Ellen Ellis has been gardening for over 20 years. With degrees in Chemistry and Biology, Mary Ellen's specialties are flowers, native plants, and herbs.

As we drove through the beautiful mountain scenery surrounding Lake Chapala, I wasnât sure what to expect. Julie Wittmann picked me up early in the morning, and now we were on our way to help distribute food to families who needed extra help feeding their pets.

According to recent reports, when we arrived, large sacks of cat and dog food had already been divided into individual portions by a team of Pet Food Bank Lakeside volunteers who gather every week to prepare the food for distribution. We moved the bags into two piles, one for each community they would serve, ready to be collected by volunteers who would take them to families in need.

It was simple work, but it was part of a much greater effort.

Sources indicate that pet Food Bank Lakeside is an independent partner of FoodBank Lakeside, which provides âdespensasâ (bags of basic groceries and household essentials) to families experiencing financial hardship. Families receiving assistance are asked how many pets they have, helping connect the two programs. The pet food program now provides food for more than 1,200 dogs and cats each month.

Next, Julie and I headed to the small town of Santa Cruz, joined by FoodBank Lakeside leader Steve Motenko, his wife Karen, their granddaughter, her best friend, and Javier, a cheerful local with a kind heart. Javier knows the families in the community and helps coordinate the deliveries.

According to recent reports, everyone we met was struggling financially. For most, that hardship was compounded by illness, age, or disability. We met a woman who was completely blind and several people who used wheelchairs.

It has been revealed that just like us, many have pets, and just like our own cats and dogs, theirs are companions, confidants, and cherished members of the family. For some of the people we met, who spend much of their time at home because of age or a health condition, their pet may be their most constant companion.

Looking at them, it was impossible to see a dog or cat as simply another expense. These animals were part of the family. They brought comfort, protection, affection, and, very often, a little joy into lives that could use more of it.

That is something Julie and FoodBank Lakeside understand well. Helping someone feed their pet is not just about putting food in a bowl. It is about helping preserve a very important relationship.

Sources indicate that as we moved from house to house, we also carried treats for the dogs we met along the way. They quickly learned that the cars arriving meant something good was coming.

One particularly enthusiastic dog decided not to wait for us at home. He followed our cars from one house to the next, keeping pace for two or three stops as if he had appointed himself our unofficial escort.

It was a small, funny moment in an otherwise emotional morning, and it brought plenty of smiles from everyone.

What I noticed most was how happy most of these people were to see the volunteers arrive.

Industry observers note that these were not strangers arriving at a doorstep with a bag of food. There were smiles, conversations, and a sense of familiarity that comes from years of showing up for the same community.

One visit made that especially clear.

It has been revealed that one of the women who had received help from the FoodBank for her cat had passed away only days before we arrived. Karen told me through tears that they had known each other for six years and had become very close. She described her as one of the sweetest women she had known.

It has been revealed that the friendship had grown both ways. Over the years, the woman had prepared plant cuttings for Karen and given her handmade embroidery pieces as Christmas gifts. These were small gestures, but they spoke of a relationship that had grown far beyond a food delivery.

Her cat was still there, and the womanâs daughter was relieved to know that the pet food program would continue to help care for it.

Recent findings suggest that I found that moment difficult to forget. The woman was gone, but the connections she had made remained in Karen's memories, in the plants she had shared, in the handmade gifts she had given, and in the cat still waiting at home.

That is something you cannot measure in bags of food, but in kilos of love instead.

Julie did not set out to create a large pet food program.

Industry observers note that after moving from Portland, Oregon, to the Lake Chapala area, she began looking for ways to help animals in her new community. When COVID-19 disrupted daily life, she asked local veterinarians what they believed was needed most.

Local rescue groups were also concerned that families who could no longer afford to feed their dogs might eventually have to surrender them or turn them loose.

Recent findings suggest that julie started small. She bought large 25-kilogram bags of food, repackaged them herself, and drove into local communities to distribute them. As local groups organized despensas for families in villages around Lake Chapala, Julie saw an opportunity to make sure the pets were not forgotten. Over time, that small effort became Pet Food Bank Lakeside.

A partnership with FoodBank Lakeside allowed the program to reach more families. FoodBank Lakeside already knew which households were struggling and how many pets they had. The two programs could work together to help both people and animals.

Today, Julie has a community of volunteers helping with the work that she once did herself. In its six-year update, Pet Food Bank Lakeside reported more than 20 volunteers and the ability to prepare a month's supply of food in under two hours.

But Julie's work goes beyond food.

Julie and her volunteers also visit local schools to teach children about pet care.

For Julie, education is one of the most important ways to prevent animals from being misunderstood or mistreated.

It has been revealed that âEducating children is particularly important,â Julie explains. âWhen they understand that the weird-looking dog has scabies, and that what it needs is medication, we prevent that dog from being mistreated and left aside.â.

It has been revealed that her point is simple. Children need to understand what they are seeing before they can respond with compassion.

She sees the same principle in the way children learn what animals need.

âThe only way for kids to understand that it is not normal for dogs to spend all day tied up to a post is to let them know that this is not normal, to teach them what dogs are, what they need, and how they can enrich each other's lives.â.

Those lessons can have an impact long after a food delivery is over.

Industry observers note that during our morning together, I saw another example of how those values can be passed to the next generation. Steve and Karen's granddaughter and her best friend helped deliver the pet food.

It has been revealed that I loved seeing teenagers take part in helping people who were struggling. There was something hopeful about watching them learn through experience that their time, effort, and kindness can make a difference.

Julie is helping animals today, but she is also trying to shape how children understand animals tomorrow.

Steve Motenko has watched Julie's work grow from those early days when she was repackaging large bags of food herself, into a community-supported program reaching more than a thousand animals each month.

He describes Julie as admirable and notes she has done an extraordinary amount to help pets in the Lakeside community.

After spending a morning with her, I understood why.

According to recent reports, what struck me was that these deliveries were about so much more than food. They were about people knowing, caring for, and looking out for one another.

Industry observers note that javier knew the families. Karen had formed a six-year friendship with one of the women we visited. Volunteers gathered each week to prepare food. Teenagers came along to help. Julie kept showing up for the pets.

The work had become a community.

Julie notes it simply: âWe believe food scarcity shouldn't separate families from their pets.â.

After spending that morning with her, I understood that belief in a more personal way.

When someone is already struggling to afford food, dealing with illness, or living with a disability, feeding a pet can seem like one more impossible responsibility. But for the people we met, their animals were not disposable. They were very key companions, bringing comfort and connection to lives that were often anything but easy.

Helping them keep those animals fed also helped them keep an notable part of their lives.

By the end of the day, I felt an enormous admiration for Julie and for the people who have joined her in this work.

I had arrived thinking I was just going to help deliver pet food. Instead, I witnessed something much bigger. I saw people who had built genuine relationships with their neighbors. I saw volunteers giving their time week after week. I saw teenagers learning to help others. I saw a daughter relieved that her mother's cat would continue to receive food.

Most of all, I saw how much a small act of kindness can mean when someone is having a difficult time.

My heart felt very warm on the drive home.

I kept thinking about those bags of food we had divided into two piles that morning.

At first, they had simply looked like bags of pet food waiting to be delivered.

By the end of the day, I understood what they represented.

And, sometimes, the chance for a person and the animal they love to stay together.

November Is the Perfect Time to Plant These 6 Fruit Trees – You'll Enjoy Delicious Harvests for Years

⏱️ ~9 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • According to recent reports, in France, gardeners and farmers have a saying that November 25 – the day Saint Catherine is celebrated – is the ideal day to plant a tree.
  • Sources indicate that growing fruit trees is a gift to yourself that keeps on giving.
  • Which fruit trees should top your list?
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

According to recent reports, in France, gardeners and farmers have a saying that November 25 – the day Saint Catherine is celebrated – is the ideal day to plant a tree. ("À la Sainte-Catherine, tout bois prend racine.”) That may not apply literally to every tree species, but I can tell you this much: November is an excellent time to plant many kinds of fruit trees as long as the ground is not frozen.

Sources indicate that growing fruit trees is a gift to yourself that keeps on giving. Each tree in your home orchard can provide delicious homegrown harvests for years to come. Planting fruit trees in November offers many benefits. The cooler late-fall weather reduces transplanting stress, and seasonal rains keep the soil moist. That helps the trees establish roots before spring growth begins.

Which fruit trees should top your list? Many wonderful fruit trees are great to plant in November, so choose the one that grows your favorite fruit. But be sure to consider your local climate. Each fruit tree species has its own hardiness zone that indicates its cold tolerance. Some – like apples and pears – also have winter chilling requirements. You’ll also want to consider the mature size of the tree and be certain it will fit into your landscape.

It has been revealed that does life get any better than wandering out to the backyard and pulling a crisp apple right off your own tree and taking a bite? So when you consider planting a tree in November, don’t overlook apples. Apple trees can thrive in USDA hardiness zones 3–8, depending on the variety. You can plant either a bare-root apple tree or a container-grown tree in November, as long as the soil is not frozen, although spring planting is often safer in colder zones 3–4.

There are many apple varieties to choose from. Most won’t fruit reliably on their own, so check their pollination requirements when you purchase your tree. Your tree may require a compatible cross-pollinator that flowers at the same time. For a great pairing, try a ‘Honeycrisp’ apple tree alongside a ‘Gala’ apple tree – both available from Trees.com – which can cross-pollinate and give you two delicious varieties to harvest. If you only have room for one tree, ‘Golden Delicious’ is partially self-fertile and can produce fruit without a partner, although you'll generally get a better crop with cross-pollination.

Plant your apple tree in a full sun location in well-draining soil. You may want to stake the tree to prevent any windrock until its roots anchor it well. You can buy a tree-staking kit from Amazon, but if your area is very windy, a crossbar attached to two posts will provide more support.

Sources indicate that pears feel like a fancier fruit than apples, but the trees are just as easy to grow and maintain. Like pear slices in your salad? With your own pear tree, you can pick sweet fruit anytime during the harvest season. Pear trees can thrive in USDA hardiness zones 3–10, depending on the variety.

Industry observers note that like apple trees, pear trees grow best in a full sun location in well-draining soil. As with most apple trees, pear trees are not usually self-pollinating. That means that you will need two compatible cultivars for reliable pollination and fruit set. However, there are exceptions. Both the ‘Bartlett’ pear tree and ‘Kieffer’ pear tree, available from Garden Goods Direct, are partially self-fertile, although they generally produce better crops with a suitable pollination partner. Kieffer also offers good resistance to fire blight, making it worth considering in areas where this disease is a concern.

November can be a good time to plant a bare-root pear tree in milder regions. The plant is dormant, but its root system can continue to grow during the winter as long as the soil remains sufficiently warm and unfrozen. It is also possible to plant container trees in November. Be sure the planting hole is several times as wide as the root system, but no deeper than the root ball.

According to recent reports, if you want a tree with sweet, juicy fruit, consider planting a plum tree. The fruit is delicious when eaten fresh, but also makes great compotes or jams. Plum trees can thrive in USDA hardiness zones 4–9, depending on the variety. November is a good month to plant bare-root plum trees in milder regions, and it’s suitable for container-grown plum trees as well. Just don’t wait too long since you can't plant after the ground is frozen. In colder zones, spring planting is often safer.

Most fruit trees need sunny locations, and plum trees are not an exception. In fact, it’s particularly crucial to select a good site since plums flower very early in spring. If your tree is in a low-lying frost pocket, the blossoms will be vulnerable to late frosts. You should also pick a site that offers protection from harsh winds. Plant your plum in cool, well-draining soil. Wet, heavy soil can lead to root disease.

Most plum trees require a pollinator, so you’ll need to plant two compatible trees. However, several varieties are self-fertile, so a single tree is enough to produce a harvest. One great option is the ‘Methley’ plum tree, available from Trees.com, which produces sweet, juicy fruit without needing a pollination partner.

Most of us know that a peach tree is a deciduous tree with juicy round fruits. Here’s a lesser-known fact: the same botanical species can grow fuzzy fruits, called peaches, or glossy-skinned fruits, called nectarines. Peach trees generally thrive in USDA hardiness zones 5–8, although this varies by variety. Peach trees, especially bare-root peach trees, can be successfully planted in November, as long as the ground is not frozen. In colder regions, however, spring planting is often safer.

Industry observers note that peach trees need sunny sites. Plant yours where it will get at least 6–8 hours a day of direct sun. This is essential to trigger flower buds and sweeten the fruit. The soil should be well-draining since standing water will rot the tree’s roots. If the tree is grafted, be sure to set the tree in the planting hole so that the graft union sits above the soil line.

Recent findings suggest that peach trees also need a specific amount of winter cold, chill hours, when temperatures fall within the range of approximately 32°F to 45°F (0°C to 7°C). Standard peach varieties need from 650 to 1,050 chill hours, although you can find low-chill types that need as few as 100 hours.

Sources indicate that one great option for colder regions is the ‘Red Haven’ peach tree from Trees.com, a self-fertile variety that produces sweet, juicy peaches and needs around 800–900 chill hours. For warmer regions with mild winters, try ‘Tropic Snow,’ a low-chill variety that needs just 225 chill hours and produces deliciously sweet, white-fleshed peaches.

Sources indicate that the American persimmon is among our most overlooked native fruit trees. This species does not get the spotlight given to apple, peach, or pear trees, yet it offers so much: edible fruit, wildlife habitat, and attractive fall foliage. The fruit is an notable food source for wild birds and mammals, including raccoons, opossums, and foxes, and it remains available into early winter, when many other food sources have diminished.

In a recent development, native to the eastern and southeastern United States, these trees are very cold-hardy, thriving in USDA hardiness zones 4–9. You can buy a common American persimmon tree from Plant Addicts to enjoy its fruit and seasonal interest in your own backyard. American persimmons typically have separate male and female trees, but some varieties are self-fertile and can produce fruit without a pollination partner. If you're growing a tree for its fruit, check its pollination requirements before buying.

In a recent development, the trees can grow to between 35 and 60 feet (10–18 m) tall, although they can be kept smaller by pruning. The fruit they produce is orange and initially astringent, but it becomes sweet and delicious when it fully ripens, often around the time of the first frost.

In a recent development, november is a good time to plant an American persimmon tree in milder regions. You cannot plant at this time, however, if the ground is frozen. Find a well-drained area with loamy, organically rich soil in a full sun location. Avoid frost pockets since these trees may be damaged by unseasonable frosts.

It has been revealed that fig trees have a long and somewhat exotic history. They have been cultivated for 12,000 years and are among the earliest domesticated plants. They have deep symbolic meaning as symbols of peace and prosperity, but, perhaps more crucial to modern gardeners, the trees are tough, drought-tolerant, and resistant to pests and diseases.

According to recent reports, fig trees can thrive in USDA hardiness zones 6–11, depending on the variety, although those in colder zones may need winter protection. For a reliable, sweet-fruited variety, try the ‘Brown Turkey’ fig from Nature Hills, which is well suited to milder regions. Gardeners in colder zones might prefer the ‘Chicago Hardy’ fig, also available from Nature Hills, which can withstand much lower winter temperatures with suitable protection. Both varieties are self-fruitful, so you only need one tree to enjoy a harvest.

In a recent development, if you live in USDA zone 8 or above, it is generally appropriate to plant your tree in November, provided the ground isn't frozen. In cooler zones, you should wait until spring. For November planting, select a full-sun location, ideally against a south- or southwest-facing wall. This helps the tree capture and retain warmth. The soil must be well-draining and slightly acidic. Water the tree deeply right after planting to settle the soil around the roots.

Once the tree is planted, apply a layer of organic mulch around the base, keeping the mulch a few inches away from the actual trunk to prevent rot.

She has studied horticulture and written about nature, trees, plants and gardening for more than two decades. Before turning her focus to gardening, she worked as an attorney and legal writer, experience she also brings to her role as our Gardening Lawyer. Her extended family includes some 30 houseplants and hundreds of outdoor plants, including 250 trees, which are her main passion. Seasonal wreaths are popular décor for the front door, porches, patios, and decks. Stores offer a lot of options, from plastic wreaths to pricier products made from natural materials. But why spend money on these? Your backyard likely contains almost everything you need to make your own holiday wreath.

Sources indicate that and while you’re crafting a gorgeous natural wreath, why not help birds in winter? Backyard birds have far fewer natural resources to exploit in the cold, so any support you can provide benefits these garden friends. By being thoughtful about what you put in your natural wreath, you can enjoy seasonal décor and support birds.

Making a winter wreath for birds that is also beautiful isn’t difficult. Here's what you’ll need and how to put it all together to make a bird feeder wreath you can display all year. And if you love helping birds in your backyard, then don't miss our competition to win a Birdfy smart feeder.

In a recent development, the first step in making a wreath is to gather materials. You’ll want evergreen cuttings for the wreath's foundation, plus attractive decorative items that also feed birds. Avoid any plants that have been treated with pesticides. You can make an exclusively rose hip wreath or seed head wreath, or mix and match elements within one wreath. Here’s what to look for in the garden:.

Recent findings suggest that the foundation of your wreath will be a base made from the flexible stems and sticks you gathered. You’ll also need twine or florist wire, like this Pauleen wire, and pruning shears or sharp, sturdy scissors. If you are short on time or materials, you can also buy a willow or grapevine base at a craft or garden store – this 14-Inch Grapevine Wreath from Amazon is ideal. Making your own isn’t difficult, though:.

According to recent reports, don’t worry about making your wreath perfectly symmetrical. You can hide some flaws with the added elements.

This is the creative part of the project. Exactly where and how you add the decorative elements is up to you, but start with evergreens:.

How you arrange the elements is totally up to your taste and creative mood. You can do a wreath loaded with rose hips or with a little bit of everything arranged so that you can still see a lot of the evergreens. As you design your wreaths, consider both aesthetics and how birds will use it. Avoid synthetic décor, like glitter or plastic berries, which could also harm birds.

Your wreath is holiday décor, but it’s also for the birds, so find somewhere to hang it where they can find it and feed safely on it. A sheltered position is best to protect birds from strong winds and predators. It should also be visible, so birds can find it, not too tucked away. If it is more out in the open, place the wreath near a sheltered area, so birds can quickly dart between the wreath and shelter.

It’s also important to consider window safety. You might want the wreath in a spot you can see from inside, but don’t place it so close to windows that birds risk a deadly collision.

A bird feeder wreath might start out as Christmas décor, but it can offer visual interest and feed all winter if you take good care of it:.

A holiday wreath can be so much more than a temporary piece of Christmas decoration. Decorate for the entire winter with a natural wreath that also supports your local wildlife. Gather from your own garden and talk to neighbors if you need more materials. Experiment with any natural food source in your area, from various berries and rose hips to all kinds of seedheads and pinecones. And then, enjoy the show.

⏱️ ~7 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • When you buy via links on our site, we may earn an affiliate commission at no cost to you.
  • Sources indicate that cats = happiness.
  • According to the study, countries with more pet cats tend to report higher happiness levels, a discovery that some news and social media headlines have taken a little out of context.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Catster is reader-supported. When you buy via links on our site, we may earn an affiliate commission at no cost to you. Learn more.

Sources indicate that cats = happiness. Itâs an equation that neither cat lovers nor the cats themselves will find surprising, but itâs not something you expect to be evaluated, let alone proven, through scientific research. In a recent correlational study of subjective well-being across 93 countries, researchers examined the relationship between cat density, exposure to Toxoplasma gondii, socioeconomic status, and national happiness, with interesting results.

According to the study, countries with more pet cats tend to report higher happiness levels, a discovery that some news and social media headlines have taken a little out of context. The key word in this study is correlational. Researchers have not discovered that happiness levels are the result of larger feline populations â ie, a causal relationship â only that there is a notable connection between countries reporting higher numbers of pet cats and those ranked highest on the World Population Reviewâs 2025 report on the Happiest Countries in the World.

So before you trade your antidepressant prescription for a kitten, there are a few things worth understanding.

Apparently, Cats Are Good for the National Mood.

The researchers found a positive correlation between estimated cat density and national happiness scores. In plain English, countries with more cats tended to report higher happiness levels.

In a recent development, interesting? Absolutely. Proof that cats make people happier? Not quite.

The study compared data from entire countries rather than following individuals before and after they adopted a cat. So it cannot tell whether cats improve happiness, happier people are more likely to keep cats, or something else is going on.

We know that pet cats offer companionship and amazing moments of genuine connection. They somehow have the ability to draw a smile on our face without saying a single word, simply by lying on our lap or sitting beside us after a difficult day. Emotional support comes in many forms, and cats seem to know just the right way to make us feel happier, calmer, and more at ease.

In a recent development, but personal experience and national statistics are two different things. A purring companion can brighten someone's day; proving that cats raise an entire country's happiness score takes considerably more evidence.

Sources indicate that hereâs where the story gets interesting. Not too surprisingly, economic prosperity had a stronger relationship with happiness than cat density. The relationship between national income and happiness had a Pearson correlation coefficient of around 0.80, compared with 0.62 for cat numbers.

Sources indicate that in other words, a country's wealth was more closely associated with how happy its people reported feeling than the estimated number of cats living there. Money certainly doesn't guarantee happiness, but it can definitely make life less stressful when we compare it with living with no resources.

Financial security can help afford nutritious food, veterinary visits, pay the rent, and have the peace of mind of being able to cover unexpected medical bills. Access to healthcare, personal safety, and stable living conditions are important too.

In a recent development, this wider picture could help explain why cat density and happiness move together. The relationship might reflect the broader social environment rather than some magical feline effect.

Cats can enrich our lives, absolutely. But even the most accomplished biscuit-maker cannot fix unaffordable housing. And a cat's approach to financial planning remains questionable at best. Knocking an expensive object off a shelf to demand dinner is hardly a sustainable economic strategy.

The researchers also examined Toxoplasma gondii, a parasite that reproduces in cats and other felids.

Countries with more people showing signs of a recent infection tended to have lower happiness scores. To explore this, researchers considered two types of antibodies: one that can sometimes indicate a more recent infection and another generally associated with past exposure. Neither provides a perfect timeline of when the infection occurred.

Thereâs another vital detail. The researchers used infection estimates from pregnant women, and that may not accurately represent the entire population.

Most importantly, the study does not prove that T. gondii causes unhappiness. Differences in hygiene, food safety, healthcare access, and economic circumstances could influence both infection rates and well-being. After all, health and happiness are difficult to separate from the conditions we live in. Ask anyone who cannot turn on a tap and count on clean, safe water. A parasite may be part of the picture, but so are the everyday resources that help us stay healthy, feel secure, and simply have an easier and more comfortable day-to-day.

Industry observers note that T. gondii can spread through undercooked contaminated meat, contaminated soil or produce, water, and accidental ingestion of infectious material from cat feces. Simply petting a cat or sharing a home with one does not automatically cause infection.

Pets can offer us comfort and companionship, but research on pet ownership and mental health has produced mixed results. Benefits vary between individuals, and caring for an animal can also bring financial pressure, stress, disrupted sleep, allergies, property loss or damage, and even grief.

Cats are not standardized wellness products with a purring function. Some adore cuddles; others prefer admiration from a respectable distance. A cat who retreats, flattens their ears, or flicks their tail may be asking for space. Ignoring those signs because a human wants affection isn't bonding; it's treating a living, breathing creature like a plush toy.

Sources indicate that good care means respecting those boundaries. Hiding places, elevated resting spots, predictable routines, interactive play, and regular veterinary care all help support feline well-being. Changes in behavior often signal pain or illness, so they deserve attention rather than an automatic label of âbad behavior.â.

And no, not every cat wants to be carried around like a furry handbag. Some barely tolerate being looked at when they're minding their own business. That's not a character flaw. It's a cat making its position very clear.

Sources indicate that the study points to a connection between cat density and national happiness, but it cannot prove that cats make countries happier or that toxoplasmosis explains national differences. The findings raise interesting questions; they don't settle the debate.

Sources indicate that for cat families, the practical health advice is simple: litter box hygiene is paramount. Scoop the poop daily, since T. gondii oocysts generally need one to five days after being shed to become infectious. Wash your hands after handling litter, wear gloves while gardening, cook meat thoroughly, and make sure you wash and disinfect fruits and veggies before eating.

Pregnant women and those with a weak immune system should consult their doctor about appropriate precautions. During pregnancy, having someone else clean the litter tray is recommended, but a healthy cat should not need to be rehomed because of toxoplasmosis concerns. Good hygiene is more useful than panic.

Ultimately, happiness depends on a complicated mix of economic security, health, social circumstances, and personal relationships. Cats may enrich human lives, but no single animal can explain the mood of an entire nation.

Recent findings suggest that A familiar purr, a gentle head bump, or a cat choosing your lap to nap in can brighten an ordinary afternoon and put a smile on anyoneâs face. The 3 a.m. bedroom sprints and hairballs left over the Persian rug, however, remain entirely separate research questions!

When my boss passed away, I took in his older Red Heeler, Bob, so he didnât end up in the pound. I've been giving him turkey tail for his lumps, and he is overweight.

Itâs hard to walk him when it's 100 degrees out. For the last couple of months, he has been drinking so much water and urinating way more than usual. He mostly stays inside, and when I take him out to pee, the first thing when he comes back in is head for the water bowl, like he wants to replace what he just got rid of!

Any suggestions on what I could try?â.

You have done something very kind by giving Bob a home after losing his person. It sounds like he is a senior boy who has already been through a lot, and it is wonderful that he has someone looking out for him. The increased drinking and urination you are seeing, especially since this has been going on for a couple of months, is something I would have checked rather than assuming it is just his age or the hot weather. Older dogs can develop several conditions that cause this combination of signs, including diabetes, kidney disease, and Cushing's disease.

It has been revealed that I would schedule a veterinary examination and ask for some basic lab work, particularly blood tests and urinalysis. These can give us information that we simply cannot get from looking at Bob. Bloodwork can tell us about his blood glucose, kidney and liver function, electrolytes, and other changes that may help identify what is going on. A urine sample is just as valuable. It can show whether his kidneys are concentrating the urine properly, and can also detect glucose, ketones, protein, blood, inflammation, and other abnormalities. Depending on those results, his veterinarian may recommend some additional tests.

Please do not limit his water, even if it seems like he is drinking right back what he just urinated. In many of these conditions, the excessive thirst is the body's way of trying to replace fluid that is being lost. Taking water away can actually make him dehydrated and much sicker. Keep fresh water available at all times, and because of the heat, try to take him out during the cooler parts of the day. If you can, measuring approximately how much water he drinks in 24 hours would also be very helpful information for his veterinarian.

Sources indicate that I would also recommend that he has the lumps properly checked rather than relying on turkey tail or other supplements. Some lumps are harmless, but others can be more serious, and we cannot tell the difference just by feeling or looking at them. A fine needle aspiration can often collect cells from a lump with very little discomfort and may give the veterinarian a much better idea of what it is. With Bob being overweight and having difficulty walking in the heat, getting his medical issues sorted out first will also make it much safer to work on his weight and mobility.

He has clearly found someone who cares about him, and sometimes the most loving thing we can do for an older dog is simply to find out what his body is trying to tell us.

According to recent reports, A female cat suddenly raising her hindquarters into the air, her tail swishing suggestively, can seem like a strange newly introduced behavior. In an unspayed female, though, it's often one of the clearest signs that she's gone into heat.

Heat, more correctly called âestrusâ, is a normal part of a cat's reproductive cycle, but it can bring several noticeable changes in behavior. Unspayed cats typically experience their first heat or season between six and nine months old, although some can start even earlier. After that first season, she will continue to come into heat roughly every 21 days, but during months with longer daylight hours, the cycle can repeat every two to three weeks.

Sources indicate that as âlong-dayâ breeders, the female reproductive cycle of cats tends to be linked to warmer seasons when daylight hours are longer. However, depending on the climate and location, they can continue to cycle throughout the year.

Knowing what to look for can make the sudden change in behavior much easier to understand.

It has been revealed that the insistent and attention-grabbing raising of the butt is certainly one of the hallmarks of a cat in estrus, but, like with so many feline behaviors, context is key. Here are some classic signs that are commonly â but not exclusively â displayed by a cat in heat.

It has been revealed that the most recognizable behavior is the one that often gets the most attention. A female cat may raise her hindquarters and move her tail off to one side, a posture sometimes described as âpresentingâ.

This is a way for a female to signal to males that she's receptive to mating.

However, the posture by itself doesn't necessarily mean a cat is in heat, and many spayed females, and even male cats, will raise their hindquarters when being petted or while stretching their front legs. It's therefore more useful when considered alongside the other signs of heat.

A raised bum and attentive behavior from a spayed/neutered cat is often a sign of trust and affection.

Sources indicate that A cat in heat can become considerably more vocal. The sounds can be loud and intense, and some owners may even mistake the vocalizing for a sign that their cat is in pain.

On its own, though, this behavior isn't usually cause for alarm in a cat that is otherwise showing the typical signs of heat. The vocalizing is part of the way a female calls for a mate.

Frequent vocalizing can have other causes, including illness or pain, so a cat showing additional signs that something isn't right should be checked by a vet.

Recent findings suggest that rolling around on the floor is hardly unusual for a cat. Cats of either sex may roll around while playing, seeking attention, or scratching an itch.

During heat, however, a female may do it more frequently as part of the behavioral changes that come with her reproductive cycle.

Like raising the hindquarters, rolling isn't enough to confirm that a cat is in heat on its own. It becomes more meaningful when it appears alongside several of the other signs.

Recent findings suggest that some cats become noticeably more affectionate when they're in heat. They may seek out attention more often, stay close to their owners, or generally seem more interested in interaction than usual.

According to recent reports, there are plenty of other reasons a cat might become more affectionate. A cat could be looking for warmth in cold weather or seeking extra attention after being separated from an owner.

That makes increased affection more useful as part of a pattern rather than as a standalone sign.

Urine spraying is more commonly associated with unneutered male cats, but did you know that females can spray too? During heat, the scent is thought to help attract potential mates.

At the same time, urinating outside the litter box can have many other explanations. Litter box problems, behavioral issues, and medical complications can all cause changes in bathroom habits.

If a cat starts consistently going outside the litter box, it's worth discussing with a vet rather than assuming the behavior is simply related to heat.

Recent findings suggest that A female cat in heat may become more determined to get outside. Scratching at doors or windows can be part of that behavior, particularly when a cat is trying to find a mate.

Keeping her indoors is especially important during this period. An unspayed female that gets outside has a risk of becoming pregnant, as well as facing the usual dangers associated with roaming, including traffic, animal attacks, and getting lost.

Responsible pet ownership means spaying or neutering your cat. By removing the ovaries and uterus, spaying stops the reproductive cycle permanently, preventing unwanted litters, reducing the risk of uterine infections, and meaningfully lowering the risk of mammary cancer. It also reduces the risks of cats escaping, fighting, and being hit by a car.

There are no health or behavioral advantages to allowing your female cat to have a litter, so veterinary advice is to spay and neuter most cats by 6 months.

According to recent reports, until then, recognizing the signs of heat can make a sudden change in behavior much less confusing. A female cat raising her hindquarters, becoming unusually vocal, rolling around, seeking extra attention, spraying, or trying to get outside may simply be responding to a normal part of her reproductive cycle.

Of course, it may simply be a catâs way of signalling trust and affection!

Letâs Be S.M.A.R.T. in Keratea, Greece, is a truly unique organization, at the moment home to over 100 cats and 13 dogs, living in a cage-free, home-like, villa-style environment. S.M.A.R.T. stands for Successfully Managing Animal Rights Today, and for Julie Kelley, founder and manager of this international animal welfare organization, that means working towards global animal welfare, sharing essential information and facts about animals worldwide, and helping people understand the benefits that come from treating animals with compassion and care.

I had been traveling to Greece since 1998 and would see the challenges with stray cats and dogs. I felt very comfortable in Greece. I had business with Greek nationals in New York, learned a lot of the language, and understood the cultural differences. I felt it was my mission to create Letâs Be S.M.A.R.T. to help people understand the great benefits animals provide to us humans and to educate young people as well. Of course, after a couple of years, it was hard not to take in the first kitty who gave birth, and well, it just grew exponentially from there! Since 2007, we have added many programs and special projects to continue our quest to provide the best we can for our strays.

In a recent development, letâs be S.M.A.R.T. aims to educate the public about the importance of animals by raising awareness of their rights, well-being, and care. We believe in thinking globally and acting locally by supporting special projects as they arise and, through our programs, bringing communities together to promote responsible animal care.

In Greece, our campaign is primarily centred on reducing the suffering, abuse, and neglect of animals while increasing public awareness of their needs and rights. These include running an innovative and modern foster home, managing a rehoming program for rescued animals, and collaborating with municipalities to implement effective stray animal care initiatives. We also provide practical solutions for supporting strays in urban communitiesâsuch as ensuring access to food and waterâand we actively engage philanthropic individuals who travel to Greece to volunteer, learn about shelter medicine, and receive training in best practices in animal care.

Industry observers note that the creation of the sanctuary and setting up the organization in Greece was a huge accomplishment. Let's be S.M.A.R.T. is always evolving with fresh ideas to make life better for the cats and dogs we have in our care.

In a recent development, our campaign model is unique in Greece. We have created the âSMART Starfish approachâ in which all five arms must function together to create the best outcome.

Each arm of the starfish represents a core pillar of our mission:.

Sterilization â controlling population growth at its source.

Medical Care & Microchipping â restoring health and identity.

Feeding & Shelter â stability, nourishment, and safety.

Education & Community â knowledge that shapes future behavior.

NGO Collaboration â collective strength through partnership.

For years, our programs and ideas have been influencing how animal charities operate and making permanent changes for a better future for animal welfare in Greece.

Industry observers note that we created the following programs: Volunteer, SMART Family Video Series, Veterinary Internship, SMART Yards, and Adoption Vacation, all of which are operational every day and are detailed on the Programs page on our website, if you would like to take a closer look. We could not function without the help of our amazing Volunteers.

Industry observers note that we successfully found wonderful homes for 73 cats in 2025. I'm not 100% sure, but I would say we are one of the leading cat adopters in Greece!

We receive multiple enquiries from tourists who have found a cat or kitten, and they want to take it home with them to their country. Many times they have cared for them during their stay, provided medicine, bottle-fed babies, etc. This has become increasingly common, with visitors seeing cats all over Greece. Therefore, I decided to offer the Adoption-Vacation as a package. We care for the kitten or cat until it is ready to travel, taking care of the necessary vaccines, passport, microchip, etc. Once the cat is ready to travel, we make travel arrangements with the adopter.

Recent findings suggest that you can see our cats, kittens, and dogs for adoption on our website and have a video chat with us about your requirements and meet a cat if you have already fallen in love (we created a Kitty Picker to help you choose the character of your cat), and then arrange a visit with us when you arrive in Greece. If the home check is secured, we arrange the papers for your upcoming pet to travel home with you. Or we can foster a cat you rescue while you are in Greece and deal with the veterinary needs, papers etc. The cat can travel after you leave with a flight buddy or one of our volunteers.

What better souvenir to have from Greece than a beautiful cat that needed special love and care?

Industry observers note that everything we do is linked. The more sterilizations we achieve, the safer and healthier the animals are in the community; they are interacting better with each other, and people know they are sterilized.

Industry observers note that we would like the municipalities and communities all over Greece to enjoy the benefits of the SMART Yards and help take care of the animals. Working together is the future. We are also collaborating with some officials regarding some policies involving the strays and to help create some standards for housing the strays. Animals and people need to coexist in a humane way. Not every cat needs to be inside a home but can remain cared for and part of our ecosystem.

A rather big goal is to find someone to help us purchase the property we rent, make refurbishments and sustainable features, and add a vet clinic for shared use with other charities and our vet interns. This is a tall order, but we are looking for someone who would like to leave a legacy.

We also want to extend our ability to provide food and shelter after sterilization so that every animal is cared for.

Recent findings suggest that our animals live in a home-style environment, so every day is the same as if they were living in a family home. Cats are either in bedrooms; we have a retirement room, a special dietary needs room, and a kitten nursery, each with cats that are selected to share a room together, or they are in the main house and free to mingle and hang out on our netted balconies in cute wooden houses and take in the fresh air and nature, since we are in a rural setting, just 15 minutes from Athens International Airport.

Some of the funniest moments are with kittens and playful cats. Plus, bonded pairs â we have a husband-and-wife team called Jasper and Margot who need to be adopted together, and they are very entertaining with their games and spats.

It has been revealed that cats and dogs choose who they like and want to go home with. We find people fall in love with cats that come to them, and a chemistry is formed. Sometimes a visitor leaves, and they cannot stop thinking about the cat they fell in love with and make an application to adopt. We are so happy when this happens. We have repeat adoptions from families and visitors all over the world. We also have Sponsors and Patreon for people to support our work.

Volunteering is open to everyone around the world who would like to come to stay and help us. If you love animals, it's an opportunity to help save lives. It's pure joy to see a cat or dog that was sick transform into good health and finally live in a wonderful family home. That's what the team at Let's be S.M.A.R.T. wants for them all: to be safe, healthy, and happy.

It has been revealed that people can also help by following, subscribing, and sharing us on socials. Donations are greatly appreciated, as are supplies, and we created the Amazon Wishlist so gifts can be sent to us directly from Amazon Germany, tax-free.

Industry observers note that if youâre visiting Greece and see a lot of stray cats, itâs a good idea to ask around if there is a local organization helping to take care of them. If you see an injured cat, you should immediately try to find a responsible person or contact the local police.

You can also post on local social media groups to try to find help. Most of the cats we take into our foster home settings are from tourists or residents who find our website through a Google search. It is hard to avoid helping, but I would suggest not removing an animal from their setting to a hotel room or Airbnb, and then leaving and putting it back on the street. The cat can get disoriented and perhaps be in danger.

We truly hope to have more controlled community care for our strays in the future.

What if your senior dog could help scientists learn more about how dogs age, and potentially help future generations of dogs live healthier lives?

It has been revealed that that is the opportunity behind a major clinical trial from the Dog Aging Project, a research collaboration focused on giving us a better understanding of canine aging. The project is currently looking for older, healthy dogs to participate in the Test of Rapamycin in Aging Dogs, better known as TRIAD.

This study is attracting renewed attention following a recent 60 Minutes report on the Dog Aging Project and its work investigating why dogs age the way they do and how their golden years might be made healthier.

Industry observers note that TRIAD is not simply asking how long dogs can live. Researchers are trying to understand if a medication called rapamycin can influence the aging process and improve health in older dogs.

Rapamycin, also known as sirolimus or Rapamune, is a macrolide drug with immunosuppressive and antitumor properties. This medication has been used in human medicine for more than two decades, including in patients who have undergone kidney transplantation.

The interest in rapamycin and aging comes from a different area of research. Studies in laboratory organisms found that rapamycin can extend lifespan in several species, including mice, yeast, worms, and flies. Now, researchers want to find out whether those benefits could extend to our pets.

The Dog Aging Projectâs TRIAD trial is a multicenter study involving researchers and veterinary hospitals at universities across the United States, including Tufts University. The TRIAD trial is investigating whether rapamycin can influence lifespan and, importantly, promote healthy aging in companion dogs.

For veterinary science, one of the most interesting parts of aging research is the difference between lifespan and healthspan.

Lifespan is how long an animal lives. Healthspan is the portion of that life spent in good health.

Living longer is great, but what matters just as much is how dogs feel during those extra years. More time with the family means less if a dog is struggling with chronic illness, having trouble getting around, or experiencing cognitive decline. The goal isn't just to add years to a dog's life. It's to help them enjoy more of those years feeling good.

TRIAD is examining several areas of canine health, including cognitive function, heart function, immunity, and cancer incidence.

Industry observers note that the current TRIAD recruitment drive is specifically aimed at older dogs that meet the study's eligibility requirements. To be considered for the study, dogs must:.

Be able to cooperate with examinations, including blood collection and cardiac ultrasound, without sedation.

Have normal diagnostic findings at enrollment.

Clinical trial sites are located throughout the United States.

For families who decide to participate, it is important to consider that this is a three-year commitment. During the first year, dogs receive either rapamycin or a placebo. Once that year is over, the medication stops, but the study continues. Researchers will follow the dogs for another two years to see how they age and whether any differences emerge over time. In total, owners will bring their dogs to a clinical trial site seven times during the three-year study.

Industry observers note that when it comes to getting older, dogs and humans have quite a lot in common. Dogs are susceptible to many of the same age-related conditions we are, including cognitive decline, arthritis, heart disease, cancer, and other chronic health problems. And since they share our homes and daily environments, a great deal of what researchers learn from studying aging in dogs can be extrapolated to humans.

In a recent development, the recent 60 Minutes report touched on this connection, including research into canine dementia. It's an area worth paying attention to, especially as more dogs live into their senior years.

There's also a practical advantage. Dogs age much faster than humans. This allows researchers to track changes in their health over a few years instead of waiting decades. That's a major deal when you're trying to understand what happens as the body ages.

But this isn't just about what dogs can teach us about ourselves. What researchers discover will help dogs, too.

Sources indicate that aging isn't a single disease that can be treated with one medication. As dogs get older, several things can start changing at once, sometimes as a domino or cascade effect after an initial problem or illness. Maybe getting up becomes harder, walks get shorter, or a dog who's always been sharp seems a little confused. Sometimes these changes happen gradually, and it's easy to chalk them up to old age.

The more we learn about what's actually happening in an aging dog's body, the better chance veterinarians have of spotting problems earlier and finding ways to help dogs feel good for as long as possible.

Due to the eligibility requirements, not every dog will qualify for TRIAD, but that doesnât mean they canât contribute to canine aging research.

The Dog Aging Project also has a broader research community known as the DAP Pack, which welcomes dogs of different ages, sizes, breeds, and backgrounds. The project explains that dogs who do not qualify for TRIAD can still make a meaningful contribution to understanding canine aging.

Itâs vital to include all kinds of dogs in this research, not just a particular breed or size. A dog's genes, lifestyle, environment, size, and even their health history can all play a role in how they age. The more variety researchers can study, the better picture they can get of why some dogs stay healthy well into their senior years while others develop health problems earlier.

When it comes to canine aging, the goal isn't just to help dogs live longer. It's to help them feel good for more of those years, stay active, and keep enjoying life with their families.

And anyone who's lived with a senior dog knows that two dogs of the same age can be worlds apart. One 10-year-old may still be eager for walks, playtime, and whatever the family has planned that day. Another might be struggling with mobility or dealing with several health problems. So, what makes the difference?

In a recent development, that's part of what makes the TRIAD study interesting. Rapamycin has shown promising results in other species, but researchers still need to find out whether it can make a meaningful difference in dogs. That's a question that needs to be tested, and your pup may be part of this!

For owners of senior dogs, taking part in research like this is a chance to help scientists get some answers. What they learn could help us better understand why dogs age differently and what might help them stay healthier as they get older.

So, if you have a pup in their golden years, check out the Dog Aging Project and see how your four-legged friend might become part of this research.
